title: Clue Two: A Knob That Turns
blurb: 1958 to about 1965. A program on a borrowed computer learns to sort cards marked left from right and the Navy expects it to be conscious, though the hype had many authors; in Buffalo the Mark I's knobs turn only when it is wrong, and you can hear it learn. A theorem's small 'if', a cheerful 'none whatever', a false clue shown in silence and a sentence about language put in the file. The candle burns about seven years: only the last knobs ever learned, and almost nobody can teach a layer in the middle.

shots.setting: Washington, D.C., 7 July 1958, a hot afternoon; the Weather Bureau's machine room

lines.direction: unhurried; a new place, a new decade

lines.text: Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron, a program on a borrowed computer, learns in fifty tries to sort cards marked left or right.
lines.direction: plain wonder, no hype; a small lift on 'learns'; 'a program on a borrowed computer' said lightly, as an aside

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Washington, 1958: in the Weather Bureau's machine room the perceptron sorts punched cards left or right, and the tally climbs to fifty. CHAPTER INDEX TAB (the film's chapter-card device for clue chapters): at the shot's first frame a manila index tab, typed in Special Elite with the chapter title 'Clue Two: A Knob That Turns', drops down from the frame's top edge at TOP-left like a file-divider tab, holds for 2.5 seconds over the picture, and slides back up (top-left, so it never shares the bottom-left corner with the date stamp); no new shot, no lamp change. Ink-bleed in from the ch02 study to a long, low machine room in labGreen backlight: a row of tall IBM 704 cabinets as black slabs with pierced vent grilles, tape drives like round eyes, a high clerestory window throwing a slanting green beam through haze (dust motes in the beam). On 'borrowed' a small tag hanging from the nearest cabinet catches the green beam: IBM 704 · U.S. WEATHER BUREAU (the 1958 learner was a program on this borrowed machine; the Mark I does not exist yet). Mid-ground: a card reader on the right whose hopper drops punch cards one at a time, each a small bright rectangle with a single notch on its left or right edge. Rosenblatt (profile, facing right, slight build, 1950s jacket) stands beside the reader, hands loose; a naval officer in a peaked cap stands behind him with hands clasped; a reporter with a notepad leans in at frame left. Camera: a slow lateral dolly left-to-right across three planes (cabinets L2, figures L3, a foreground cable run L5). A paper tally in Special Elite type in the lower right (its numerals are part of the prop, not a caption) counts the cards 1 to 50 as they fall from 'perceptron' (one tick per card, on twos), and above the reader a small two-lamp panel marked LEFT / RIGHT: for the first dozen cards the lamps flicker inconsistently; after about card 30 the correct lamp lights every time (left-notched card: LEFT; right-notched card: RIGHT; it is sorting cards, not learning the idea of direction), and at 50 the reporter's pencil starts to move. Date stamp bottom left as L0302 begins (the index tab hangs top-left, so the two never share a corner). Name card for Rosenblatt on first appearance.

shots.setting: Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, Buffalo, New York, 1958–60, night; the Mark I installation

lines.text: In Buffalo, Rosenblatt built it as a machine: an eye, random wires, and motor-driven knobs. Each knob sets how strongly one wire counts: its weight.
lines.direction: slow, naming each part as the camera reaches it; a small stress on 'machine' (the 1958 learner was a program; this is the hardware); then plainly, defining: 'how strongly one wire counts'; a small warm stress on 'weights', a word we will keep

lines.text: When it was wrong, only the knobs of lit wires turned, a little, toward the answer.
lines.direction: precise, teacherly; slight weight on 'wrong' and 'lit'

lines.text: You could hear it learn. I love that.
lines.direction: hushed delight; "I love that" is the teacher's own aside, smiling, almost to himself

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Buffalo: the Mark I's photocell eye, its harp of random wires and its motor-driven knobs; on each mistake only the lit wires' knobs turn, and you can hear it learn. The film's first great machine image. The markIPerceptron set: a row of grey 1950s cabinets as backlit silhouettes. A dolly from left to right along the installation (three parallax planes, fog sheet between L2 and L3). (1) The eye on its stand: a 20×20 grid of photocells, lit from inside, aimed at a card. (2) The cabinet stencilled MARK I, doors open: the patchboard as a harp of hundreds of patch cords, backlit so every cord is a dark string against green light, wired at random (seeded, no pattern). (3) The rack stencilled PERCEPTRON: rows of potentiometer knobs, each with its own small motor housing, each knob sitting on one of the last wires, between the association units and the response dial (the random wires behind them have no knobs and never change). On 'weight' the camera eases close on one knob and its single string: it turns a notch and the string thickens, then thins, so the eye sees that a knob is how strongly one wire counts. Then the camera settles and the teaching machine takes over the same frame: perceptronRetina, driven by its real training record (horizontal vs vertical bars, the rule applied only on mistakes). A card lands on the retina; bright wires show the lit cells feeding the association units that fire; the dial swings; when the answer is wrong, ONLY the lit knobs rotate (each by its real Δw) and their loom strings to the response dial thicken (warm for +, cool for -). Unlit knobs never move; on a correct answer nothing moves at all. A small caption: 'illustration: the perceptron rule, run for real'. The tally readout ('presentation n · mistakes in the last 20') counts down as it learns. On 'hear it learn' the picture holds still and only the motors move, each turn a tiny whirr that the score picks up. The camera stays on the machine through the whole hold (the wiring question card comes down in ch03-s05's board beat, not here). Date stamp bottom left in Special Elite.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a parchment plate inks the learning rule and a dividing line that jumps on mistakes and settles; then IF is circled and a new question card goes up on the thread. CAMERA: plate, then a tilt up to BOARD (the Q1 swap as a 1–2 s insert). Paper-fold transition to a parchment plate in ink. Top: the rule sets in KaTeX, w ← w + η·t·x, with three small ink labels underneath (weight, step, right answer × input). Below: a square plot with a scatter of small ink dots (circles = one kind, crosses = the other), separable. A straight ink line starts at a bad angle and, with each mistake, jumps (on twos) to a new angle; after a handful of jumps it settles cleanly between the two kinds and stops. On 'If one exists' the word IF is circled in ink in a margin note, and the plate's line freezes. Then, in the music-only hold, the camera tilts up off the plate to the case board, and as it reaches the board the light tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood, 1.2 s, no dip) from labGreen to candleAmber (STUDY LOCK: study, board, shelf and Wall are always candleAmber; era colour stays only in practicals). BOARD MAP (canonical, from the staging appendix; repeated word for word): the Case Board is a fixed grid of slots laid out as network columns by era, left to right: C1 (1943–1969) the far-left input column, C2 (1969–1997), C3 (2006–2017), C4 (2018–2023), and the output, the glowing chat box, at the far right; the case card WHO TAUGHT IT? hangs in slot K at the board's centre; the suspect cards S1 RULES, S2 KNOWLEDGE and S3 LEARNING hang in the left margin, top to bottom; the founding row F1–F2 runs beneath columns C3 and C4; the question-card thread runs along the board's top edge (slots Q1 to Q4, left to right), a low-chroma oxblood string (emberRed rim mixed about 60% into candleAmber) that glints only where the lamp's pool falls; the Wall of Forecasts hangs to the board's right, its slots W1 to W8 left to right (W1 Turing, W2 chess, W3 Rosenblatt 1961, W4 Florence 2012, W5 Coulom, W6 the 30-to-50-years slip in shadow, W7 Hinton 2017, W8 an empty pin until ch15). At thread slot Q1, the far-left end of the oxblood thread, the hands first unpin the card from ch02, HOW COULD A NET REWIRE ITSELF? (answered: a knob that turns), and let it drop into the lamp's pool; then they pin the new card in the same slot, Q1: AND IF NO STRAIGHT LINE EXISTS? It sways a little and holds, music only, long enough to read (31 characters).

lines.text: A magazine asked what use it was. “At the moment, none whatever,” Dr. Rosenblatt said cheerfully. And what could it never do? “Love,” he said. “Hope. Despair.”
lines.spoken: A magazine asked what use it was. “At the moment, none whatever,” Doctor Rosenblatt said cheerfully. And what could it never do? “Love,” he said. “Hope. Despair.”
lines.direction: enjoy the first half; this is the most likeable man in the chapter. Then 'And what could it never do?' a gentle turn, and the quotation lower and slower, without a smile: 'Love,' a breath, 'he said', then 'Hope.' and 'Despair.' each set down alone

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Rosenblatt shrugs his cheerful 'none whatever'; asked what it could never do, he answers LOVE · HOPE · DESPAIR, and the card lands on the spoken words and is read in full; then a pan to the Wall, where the chess slip is pinned in W2. CAMERA: stage, then a pan right to WALL (the W2 pin). Cut back to the candle's pool; under the cut the light tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood, 0.7 s, no dip) from the board's candleAmber to the stage's labGreen. In the pool: Rosenblatt in profile, his hand rising open as if presenting nothing at all (a cheerful shrug, a hand-sprite swap to 'open' on the quote). The quote is spoken, so no card for it. Then, as the narrator asks what it could never do and reads his answer ('Love,' he said. 'Hope. Despair.'), he throws up his hands (both arms rise, held on twos), and three words lift beside him one at a time like sparks, on a small card whose one-line attribution beneath gives the question he was answering (so the words are never read as a claim that the machine feels): LOVE · HOPE · DESPAIR, then the short line '— Rosenblatt, on its limits (New Yorker, 1958)' (quoted verbatim with its 'he said', as the magazine printed it; the source stays on the card, like every other reported quote; the full exchange is in creditsSources), held together, music only, until the whole card has been read. After that the camera pans right off the stage to the Wall of Forecasts beside the case board, and as it reaches the Wall the light tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood, 1.2 s, no dip) from labGreen to candleAmber (STUDY LOCK: study, board, shelf and Wall are always candleAmber; era colour stays only in practicals) (its slots W1 to W8 left to right: W1 Turing, W2 chess, W3 Rosenblatt 1961, W4 Florence 2012, W5 Coulom, W6 the 30-to-50-years slip in shadow, W7 Hinton 2017, W8 an empty pin until ch15). The hands pin the chess slip in slot W2, just right of Turing's slip in W1. The slip is fresh white; a small due-date tag hangs from its pin. Further along the wall, beyond the lamp's reach, the corner of one older slip hangs half-lit in shadow (slot W6, unread). The slip reads SIMON & NEWELL · CHESS CHAMPION BY 1968. Hold on the slip to the end of the shot, long enough to read it (order: sparks and card read, then pan and pin, then the slip read; the beats carry the clock). SCRIPT NOTE (review round 1): L0312 now voices the answer (q-rosenblatt-love), so the card lands on the spoken words, not in silence; the hold is about 5 s shorter, so the pan to the Wall comes about 4.8 s after the line ends.

The 1958 candle on its stage, lower now: about seven rings have burned away, and they stand above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Figures leave the pool one by one, walking out of frame on twos (no moonwalking): the reporter, the officer, then Widrow, who pauses at the rim and turns toward a small antenna silhouette on the horizon before going.
